comment: What each kind of model call needs, and which proxies may serve it.
Proxies are tried in the listed order and the first one holding a credential wins, so this
list is both the permission list and the preference order. A proxy absent from a use case
cannot serve it even when its credential is present.
Model names live with the proxy in model_proxies.json. Add a proxy name to an order below
only when that proxy should serve the use case.
openai_compatible is served only on a self-hosted install whose operator set a model address.
It comes before the proxies that hold a key, so an operator who points the install at their
own model does not have a call go to a cloud provider because an older key is still set.

agent_run.comment: OpenAI is the base model for user-facing agent runs; Anthropic is the fallback and the gateway routes to GLM 4.6. The base model costs less per token for the same work, and on scheduled-trigger sessions, the heaviest shape, it is also faster and completes at least as often. Interactive Slack chat has the least evidence, so watch Slack completion and measure again before a change here. openai_codex leads the order and changes nothing for a deployment that holds no ChatGPT token: it is only ever present as a workspace's own subscription, and a workspace that signed one in expects its runs to spend that subscription.
agent_run.reasoning_level_comment: Medium when a person is waiting on the answer. At effort high the model thinks hard on every step, and thinking tokens can be half of a run made of simple, repeated steps. Adaptive thinking still digs in on hard steps at medium. The Slack channel uses medium for the same reason. Read by runtime-platform/model_resolver.ts, which applies reasoning_level_when_nobody_is_waiting to trigger runs.
agent_run.reasoning_level_when_nobody_is_waiting_c: A scheduled or app-event run has nobody watching a spinner, so its only cost is money, and the automation packs were measured at this level. Applies to trigger_type schedule and app_event; a person's message, an API call, a manual run and a Slack turn are all somebody waiting.
agent_run.prompt_cache_retention_comment: Long. The 1-hour TTL bills cache writes at 2x base against 1.25x for the 5-minute one, so the 5-minute entry looks cheaper on any benchmark that starts each task in a fresh session — every write is cold there and the discount is all upside. Real traffic is the opposite shape: the prefix is already warm and the only question is whether it is still alive when the next run arrives. The gaps between two runs of one session are human-paced, so a 5-minute entry usually expires before the next run and a 1-hour entry usually survives, which makes the short retention the more expensive one. Measure again if the gap distribution changes.
agent_run.stream_idle_timeout_ms_comment: Tool calls have a deadline and the model call needs one too: without it, a provider stream that stops producing holds the run open while the worker keeps its lease, so the stale-run reaper correctly leaves it alone and the person sees a spinner and then a bare failure. This is the deadline for silence, not for the answer. It sits above the largest gap between two events of a healthy run, which is far above the typical gap of a few seconds. Measure the gaps before lowering it; a slower model or a heavier reasoning level moves the distribution.

session_summary.comment: Session-history compaction and the Slack turn synthesiser. Both rewrite or restate history rather than continue a conversation, so neither needs the session's model: a summary produced on the agent-run model was billed at agent-run rates with the session's reasoning level still on. OpenAI leads because gpt-5.6-luna is a cost tier rather than an agent-run tier, and compaction runs on every long session. Changing the model here moves the Slack synthesiser too — it is the other caller.

onboarding_scan.comment: The pre-onboarding company scan: the evidence about one company in, one JSON brief with the first job offers out. These offers are the first thing a new customer reads, and a weak or untrue one loses them, so it leads with Claude Opus 5.5: on the onboarding-check set it wrote more offers that fire on an event and fewer untrue ones than the fast gateway model, for about three seconds more. Opus 5.5 always thinks and its thinking counts against the output limit, so the limit leaves room for it and reasoning is low. The gateway model and OpenAI stay as fallbacks.

slack_discovery.comment: The Slack workspace sweep: one small structured call per channel to say what that channel is about, then one call over those digests to propose scheduled workflows. Nobody is waiting behind a spinner, but a workspace with fifty channels makes fifty of these, so it is shaped for cost: reasoning off, one short structured answer, the same cheap proxy order as the onboarding scan. One use case covers both calls because they are the same shape; split it the day the proposal wants a smarter model than the digest. Infrastructure, not an agent run: no workspace picks this model and no BYOK key pays for it, so model_access is left unset the way titles and the onboarding scan do.

slack_workflow_proposal.comment: The proposal half of the Slack sweep: one call over every channel digest that has to return a structured list of workflows worth running. GLM through the gateway answered the digests fine and then could not produce valid structured output for this schema, so this one leads with OpenAI and keeps the gateway as the fallback. The digests stay cheap on slack_discovery.
